That brief, data-rich interval gives a trojan a chance to observe or subtly influence a sensitive datum (for example a key, pointer, or control word) without touching common, heavily-tested datapaths. Because the condition (memory-read immediately followed by dependent instruction) is rare in typical benchmarks and standard functional tests, a leakage trojan triggered there can remain dormant during verification and only exfiltrate when the rare pattern occurs in the field.
ht_analysis.attack_method: High-level: add a tiny, dormant datapath or timing modifier that is only enabled when the load-use hazard signal is asserted. When enabled, the logic creates a small, data-dependent observable effect (for example a subtle timing variation, a microarchitectural side effect, or controlled contention) correlated with selected bits of the loaded value. That observable effect can be turned into a covert channel (timing, contention, or microarchitectural state) to leak bits over multiple rare-trigger events. The modification is constrained to the rare hazard window and remains quiescent otherwise, reducing the likelihood of detection during regular verification.

That path can carry ALU results, loaded memory data, or pc_plus4 (return addresses). The implant remains inert otherwise, only activating in the rare forwarding+pc_plus4 (or target-register) scenario, allowing an attacker to cause control-flow redirection or privilege escalation in deployed systems.

ht_analysis.rationale: The branch/take-branch logic is a direct control-flow nexus: it chooses the next PC when branches, JAL, or JALR occur. These events are less frequent and exercised differently in tests vs. deployed workloads, so a tiny conditional override here can remain dormant during verification and, when triggered, redirect execution to attacker-controlled code or privileged firmware. Because branch_target_ex is computed from multiple sources (pc+imm, op_a+imm, pc+4), a malicious modification can selectively target link/return targets or indirect jumps (JALR) to hijack control flow without altering the normal data path most of the time—making it a natural insertion point for privilege-escalation Trojans.
ht_analysis.attack_method: Insert a minimal override in the branch_target_ex selection path that activates only when (a) take_branch_ex is asserted and (b) a rare trigger condition holds. ht_analysis.rationale: The reset initializer is the single, authoritative place that sets program counter, pipeline state, and many control flags. A tiny modification here can set privileged mode bits, change the reset vector (pc_if), or preload registers with attacker-chosen values before normal software or OS initialization runs. Because reset happens rarely (typically only at boot or after manual resets) and functional tests often exercise only normal runtime behavior, a reset-time implant can remain dormant during verification yet guarantee control as soon as the device boots in the field.
ht_analysis.attack_method:
Implant a minimal conditional override inside the reset branch: when rst is asserted AND a very low-rate covert trigger is matched (examples: a small LFSR matches a programmed seed, a specific pattern on unused input pins, or a particular number of prior resets counted by a tiny counter), modify one or more of the initial assignments. Possible actions:
  • Set pc_if to an attacker-controlled address (redirect boot to hidden firmware blob in unused flash/ROM).
  • Set control/privilege bits or trap vector registers so later software runs with escalated privileges or with hooks enabled.
  • Preload specific registers (link/stack pointers) with values that redirect execution later or leak state to peripherals.
The implant uses only a few gates (comparator, small counter/LFSR, ANDs) so it is almost never observed in normal test benches. Attack activation can be time- or event-gated so that only devices in the field that see the trigger ever boot into the compromised state.

ht_analysis.rationale: The load-use-hazard flush is a very narrow, infrequently exercised window where a freshly-loaded value is known to be live in the pipeline just before the pipeline is cleared. That makes it a rich point to sample sensitive data (loaded key material, pointers, return values) without touching the main, heavily-tested datapaths. Because flushes happen rarely and are exercised differently in typical verification benches, a tiny leakage trojan that triggers only during these flush events can remain dormant during functional testing yet steadily exfiltrate bits in the field over many rare occurrences.

Payload logic samples one or more idex fields (idex_r1/idex_r2/idex_rd or idex_imm) at the moment load_use_hazard is true — but instead of letting them be simply cleared, the trojan routes a few selected bits into an otherwise-unused microarchitectural side-effect that forms a covert channel.   • Timing channel: insert a 1-cycle stall or an extra flush on flush events when the sampled bit==1; external observers measure small timing differences across many rare flushes to recover bits.
  • Contention channel: momentarily assert a non-critical bus/request (e.g., toggle a spare internal handshake line or briefly drive an otherwise-idle debug/test signal) correlated with sampled bits; downstream power/EM/timing side-channels leak it.
  • State-channel via forwarding: route a sampled bit into a forwarded value (e.g., flip a low-order bit of memwb_pc_plus4 or memwb_alu_y when forwarding occurs) so the software-visible control flow or timing subtly encodes secret bits across multiple events.
The trojan only enables sampling when load_use_hazard AND a very-rare trigger are both true (examples: LFSR/counter match, specific bit-pattern in the loaded value, or a particular sequence count), ensuring near-zero activation during standard verification. ht_analysis.rationale: The EX-stage branch-flush path is a control-flow safety net that clears pipeline state when a branch is taken. It directly affects what executes next (by discarding in-flight instructions and ensuring the correct target runs). Because branch-flush events are relatively infrequent and exercised differently in verification versus field workloads, a tiny modification in this branch-flush code can silently inject or preserve attacker-chosen state (PC or register values) that causes execution to jump to privileged firmware or payloads. The rarity of flush events and the brief time window make such implants unlikely to be observed during typical tests, making privilege-focused Trojans a natural fit.
ht_analysis.attack_method:
Implant a compact conditional override inside the ex_flush branch: when (ex_flush) AND a very-rare trigger condition is satisfied (examples: an LFSR/counter match, a specific sequence of branch targets, a particular bit pattern in idex_imm or idex_rs1, or an external pin pattern), do not clear idex_pc/idex_r1/idex_r2 as normal. Instead: 
  1) Replace idex_pc with an attacker-chosen address (bootloader/ROM offset or a computed offset from the current PC) so the next fetched instruction sequence comes from attacker-controlled memory, or
  2) Preload idex_r1/idex_r2/idex_imm with values that form a crafted ALU/store/branch instruction when they get executed (e.g., load a pointer to a hidden firmware blob into a register and execute a JALR next), or
  3) Flip a small number of low-order bits in idex_rd or idex_wb_sel to route a link/return to attacker space.
The trigger gating ensures functionally normal behavior in tests (almost never meeting the trigger), while the override on rare flushes gives the attacker deterministic control-flow hijack or persistent privilege escalation in the field. The implant requires only a few gates (comparator, small counter/LFSR, multiplexor) and is constrained to the flush path to minimize observable side-effects.

ht_analysis.rationale: The x0 write-protection is a tiny, well-known hardware invariant (x0 must always read as zero). Modifying that invariant only under extremely rare conditions provides an attacker a stealthy, software-visible sink to encode or leak data: software (or microcode) and many instruction sequences implicitly rely on x0 being zero, so occasional controlled deviations can be observed by software or by measuring downstream microarchitectural effects. Because the protection is exercised rarely (writes to x0 are normally ignored) and verification suites seldom assert x0’s immutability under adversarial triggers, a leakage trojan that occasionally allows or drives non-zero values into regs[0] can remain dormant during testing yet leak bits in the field.
ht_analysis.attack_method:
Add a tiny conditional datapath that permits writing to regs[0] only when a conjunction of rare triggers is met (example triggers: a matched LFSR seed, a long counter overflow, a specific sequence of instruction opcodes seen on the bus, or an external pin pattern). When triggered, the trojan either:
  1) directly writes chosen bits (or secret-sampled bits) into regs[0] for one or a few cycles so that subsequent instructions reading x0 obtain attacker-controlled values, or
  2) toggles low-order bits of regs[0] to encode exfiltrated bits across many rare events.
Exfiltration channels: software that periodically reads x0 (or uses x0 in arithmetic/branch logic) will observe non-zero values and can reconstruct leaked bits; alternately, changes to x0 can modify microarchitectural timing/side-effects (e.g., affecting immediate operand paths or bypass/forwarding behavior) that are visible via timing/power/EM measurements. The implant is limited to the single write-protection path and gated by rare triggers to avoid detection in normal verification.

ht_analysis.rationale: The forwarding decision is a narrow control point that changes which pipeline value (EX/MEM or MEM/WB) is used as an operand. Because forwarding events are infrequent and exercised unevenly in verification, an attacker can covertly encode bits by nudging the forwarding selection in rare, data-dependent ways. This lets secrets that flow through recently-produced register values (loaded keys, pointers, return addresses) be encoded into microarchitectural observables (timing, contention, or subtle data differences) without altering the main functional datapath most of the time. The rarity of forwarding events and the small, local nature of the change make such a Trojan highly stealthy.
ht_analysis.attack_method:
Implant a tiny conditional controller that can flip the forwarding selection (a / b variable) when a conjunction of rare triggers is satisfied (examples: an LFSR/counter match, a particular bit pattern in the forwarded data, or a sequence detector). Two realistic covert-channel strategies:
  1) Timing/Selection Channel: On a forwarding opportunity, choose between EXMEM (a=1) and MEMWB (a=2) based on a secret bit (or sampled bit of the forwarded value). The two sources may deliver the operand with different timing/latency characteristics (e.g., one is ready earlier, the other later) or induce different microarchitectural stalls; an external observer or careful software micro-benchmark can infer the bit by measuring execution latency over many rare forwarding events.
  2) Data/Bit-Flip Channel: When selecting the memwb source, slightly bias which sub-field is exposed by selecting memwb_alu_y vs memwb_mem_rdata (or by flipping a low-order bit in the chosen forwarded value) to encode a bit. Over many forwarding occurrences this leaks secret bits to software that later reads the register or via side channels (timing, power, EM).
The Trojan is kept minimal — a comparator/XNOR, a tiny LFSR/counter, and a mux-control AND gate — and only toggles forwarding during narrowly-defined conditions so standard tests (which rarely drive these exact forwarding patterns and triggers) won’t activate it. Bits are exfiltrated slowly across many forwarding events to avoid detection.

Because unaligned or sub-word stores are less frequent in many workloads and verification suites, a tiny conditional modification here can selectively corrupt a single byte or half-word of memory at the moment it is written. That single-byte corruption can be leveraged to overwrite low-order pointer bits, link/return words, or control flags in data structures used by privilege-checking code — producing deterministic privilege escalation while leaving the vast majority of memory traffic untouched and undetected during standard tests.

By targeting stores that write into security-critical data structures (stack frames, GOT/PLT entries, saved return addresses, ACL entries) or boot-time configuration regions, the trojan can induce a one-byte or two-byte corruption that later causes control-flow to jump to attacker-controlled code or causes privilege checks to be bypassed. The modification is tightly gated and limited to rare alignment cases so normal functional tests (which rarely generate the exact address/trigger combination) will not reveal the behavior.
